newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem killed in village fight with Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Moslem killed in village fight with Serbs.

text.p: A Moslem was killed and two Serbs were injured during fighting in a disputed village in northeast Bosnia on Tuesday before NATO peacekeepers intervened, a NATO spokesman said.

Major Brett Boudreau said Russian and American soldiers separated the two sides in the village of Gajevi, where Moslem refugees are trying to return to their homes, and disarmed Serb police carrying illegal AK-47 rifles.
The flareup angered NATO, which accused the Bosnian government of fomenting violence by sending refugees back to the village on Serb territory without prior agreement.
"We believe this to be a deliberate, orchestrated and provocative move to circumvent established procedures for the return of refugees," NATO spokesman Major Simon Haselock said.
Around 600 Moslems, including women and children, entered Gajevi in northeast Bosnia on Monday. The village is in the Zone of Separation (ZOS) between Serb and government-controlled territory.
Refugee men who remained in the village overnight said they were forced to flee by up to 300 Serbs firing rocket-propelled grenades and small arms before before fleeing.
Boudreau said there was no evidence that mortars were fired, as both sides claimed.
Bosnian Serb deputy Interior Minister Milenko Karisik blamed the Moslems for starting the fighting by firing on Serb police.
The ZOS is an area on either side of former front lines in Bosnia within which NATO has wide-ranging authority under the terms of the Dayton peace agreement.
Gajevi is inside the zone but on the Serb side of what is known as the Inter-Entity Boundary Line (IEBL), which separates Moslem-Croat and Serb-held territory in Bosnia.

NATO suspected that both Serb and Moslem troops were involved in the incident and local NATO commander, U.S. General Montgomery Meigs, had ordered the military on both sides to get their men under control.
The U.N. refugee agency said none of the returnees had been approved under an internationally-supervised application process agreed by the formerly warring parties.
Shooting on Monday wounded at least one Serb.

Whoever provoked the Gajevi incident, refugee officials acknowledge the Dayton peace agreement's promise that refugees would be able to return to their homes across de facto ethnic boundary lines has not been fulfilled.
Several million people were uprooted during the war, some fleeing to other safer parts of Bosnia and others taking refuge in Europe or countries further abroad.
As many as 250,000 of those refugees and displaced persons have returned voluntarily during 1996, but virtually none of them have gone home to areas controlled by rival ethnic groups.
Serb leaders, who control the 49 percent of Bosnia known as Republika Srpska, are vociferous in their determination to maintain the "ethnically cleansed" territory they fought for.

"The ZOS is the only area in Bosnia where minorities can return because NATO has the ultimate say there, not the Bosnian Serbs, who normally oppose returns," said Kris Janowski, Sarajevo spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency.
"There is complete hostility towards returns in Republika Srpska and indeed there is no process for return to Republika Srpska since there's no cooperation by the authorities."
